title: In the shadow of fear
author: Shelley Walia
content_html:
As a war-torn West Asia trembles under the weight of relentless conflict, its devastation spills across the globe, inflating the price of bread and deepening the suffering of the poor. One is reminded that fear travels far beyond the battlefield, seeping deep into the ordinary rhythms of life.

It is in this climate of dread that I find myself sitting on the banks of Lake Lucerne, in a village called Brunnen. Across the water I can see the Bürgenstock, the high mountain and luxury alpine resort, where J.D. Vance is said to have met the Iranian delegation in search of some resolution to the crisis between Iran and America. The bright day is darkening into evening, a cool wind moving in steadily, and in my lap lies Alan Paton’s Cry, the Beloved Country, a novel I have returned to after many years. Some books simply do not age. They deepen their hold instead.

And so, this evening, I find myself thinking of Paton’s novel, so often read as a lament for apartheid, but which is also something more enduring in the form of a meditation on what fear does to a nation, and to the child not yet born who inherits that unwarranted fear. That warning feels uncannily contemporary tonight, as I sit anguished at the world’s unbridled belligerence, its sectarian violence, and the merciless toll of Ukraine, Gaza, and Iran.

As I read, my mind travels southward to apartheid South Africa, to the long brutality that Alan Paton had spent his life resisting. And then, almost by accident, I find something I had completely forgotten, a yellowing newspaper cutting tucked into the back of the book, a piece by Anne Paton, Alan Paton’s wife, entitled Fly, My Beloved Country. It was written nearly three decades ago, describing why she had been compelled to leave the country she loved. She had never wanted to leave. But it had become impossible to stay. I sensed intense grief in that statement.

It is not Paton’s novel alone that haunts me now. It is the imagined, almost mythic, departure of Anne Paton from a continent already scarred by injustice. In my mind, her exit becomes a mirror of another great African farewell. Karen Blixen’s Out of Africa reminds me of the touching scene where, after the death of her lover, Denys Hatton, she sits in a small plane, looking down at the endless savannah, the animals moving in silent procession.  In my memory, the haunting notes of Mozart’s Clarinet Concerto in A Minor swirl around her, its music at once tender and desolate, as though carrying the weight of leaving itself. The clarinet, an instrument of call and response, mirrors the dialogue between the departing individual and the land she leaves behind. It seems to ask, “Will you remember me?” and answers, “I will, even if I cannot stay.”

Reading Anne Paton again during my sojourn here surrounded by the Uri Alps in a quaint village on the lake, I am struck by the dignity of Anne’s grief. Overwhelming rage and accusations would have been the usual response. But her departure resonates, inevitably, with a sense of the loss of a beloved country as the land recedes, still beautiful, still beloved, but no longer inhabitable. The moment of departure has always stayed with me as an ache of a dream that ruptures, the lover gone, the farm lost, the illusion of settlement undone. 

Personal elegy

The film and book Out of Africa blend in my imagination resounding with the concerto arousing the gloom of Anne and Karen, both suspended between earth and sky, watching a world they loved and lost, and wondering whether any of it will ever be whole again. That image has become, for me, a personal elegy for every departure, every forced or chosen exile that leaves behind a landscape of both beauty and longing.

From England, where I was then based, the news from South Africa began to arrive in fragments, images of violence, of social breakdown, of a state increasingly unable to guarantee safety. This was no longer the South Africa of freedom one had dreamt of, nor even the morally legible brutality of apartheid. It was something far more dispiriting. 

To love a country in such a moment is to experience that love as pain. Anne Paton’s admission captures the tragedy of nations that fail those who love them most. Departure, in such cases, becomes a compulsion, a breakaway, a form of interior exile.

For me, this is not a story confined to South Africa. It is a pattern that recurs across societies where political freedom arrives without the institutional and moral structures required to sustain it. And that is Paton’s enduring relevance. To love a country deeply is to risk being wounded by it. The greater the attachment, the sharper the loss. Perhaps that is the most difficult truth of all.

It returns now when I think of Anne Paton, the same quiet devastation, the same reluctant severance. Life continues, as it must, but something irrevocable has been left behind. As I close this piece, I hear, in my mind, that distant clarinet. It reminds me that every departure carries with it a promise of return, however distant, and that the landscapes we leave behind continue to shape us, long after we have gone. In remembering Anne Paton’s flight, and in recalling Blixen’s solitary plane ride, I am reminded that to love a place is to accept its inevitable loss, and to mourn that loss is, in its own way, a tribute to the enduring beauty of the beloved country.

I kept that newspaper cutting. I carry it still.

title: More than just a ride
author: Shreya  Sundar
content_html:
As I sit back and picture my college days, the endless and crowded bus journeys vividly cross my mind. What started out as the most tiresome part of the day soon became a routine with a tad bit of comfort. With a huge crowd huddled at the bus stop during the peak hours of the day,it truly felt like the survival of the fittest, those who were strong battled their way into the bus while the meek were left behind on an endless pursuit of waiting for the next bus.

Amid all this chaos, the wave of happiness that set in at the sight of an empty bus was simply unexplainable. Yet, the fight for the window seat remained eternal, the calculated moves people made to secure a seat in a crowded bus was something to be appreciated. The most memorable rides were the one with friends whose presence made me forget the long journey as we chatted our way through the rides filled with gruelling traffic.

A mode of transport that brought to light people from different backgrounds. One could see college students in their own world with ear plugs blaring music loud enough to cancel out the hums of human activities, school children clinging to their parents hoping not to be squished by the crowd, corporate employees lost in their thoughts, flower vendors bringing a beautiful scent into the bus with a bag full of blossoms large enough to block the aisle and then came the conductor tirelessly shuttling back and forth through the packed aisle making sure everyone gets a ticket; which was almost a live example of how determined humanity can be.

It was not just a ride but a lesson in resilience and patience. Consumed by my college life such things often went unnoticed but deep down inside subconsciously it had a profound impact that would be cherished forever more.

title: Toilet travails
author: Seetha Jayakumar
content_html:
The journey is about the destination, they say. I beg to differ. Sometimes, it’s about the toilet breaks in between. We are on a trip with a group of friends, ticking one more tourist destination off our bucket list. The mood on the tourist bus is joyful and everyone is buzzing after the hearty breakfast we just had, except me.

“Hope there are toilet breaks in between,” I say as soon as I settle down. I silently scold myself for all the tea I drank.

“Are you here for a holiday break or a toilet break?” my college-going daughter teases.

“Can’t enjoy the first one without the second,” I say.

I am not obsessed with toilets, but years of road trips across the country have left me acutely aware of one truth — a beautiful holiday can quickly become miserable if there isn’t a decent toilet break when you need one.

“Don’t worry, Amma. I think there is a toilet on the bus,” comforts my daughter.

“It’s not working, madam,” says the driver before I could let out a relieved phew.

My bladder starts misbehaving immediately. The bus is air-conditioned, set perhaps at the lowest possible temperature point, for god knows why. The place we have to go to is a good three hours away. It’s all psychological, I tell myself. Just don’t think about it.

“We’ll stop at a toilet on the way,” says the driver.

I heave a huge sigh of relief. My husband lets out a cackle. “It’s different for you guys. You can go wherever you want,” I grumble.

The road to our destination is beautiful. Lush green hills roll past us and tiny streams sparkle in the sunlight. While everyone is oohing and aahing at the scenery, all I can think of is that toilet waiting somewhere for me. True to his words, the driver stops the bus at a small roadside food court with a cute eatery and a toilet tucked away at the back. The bus empties all of a sudden, people queuing for either food or the toilet. By the time I climb down from my middle seat (specially selected for comfort and motion sickness), there’s already a long queue outside the ladies’ toilet. The men’s queue moves quickly. Before my turn comes, the bus driver signals it’s time to leave.

“Hurry up, madam. We have to be there in one hour if we want to make it time for the boat rides,” he says.

With a heavy heart and an even heavier bladder, I hurry back to the bus. My husband and my daughter are already in their seats, munching on pakoras and sipping cool drinks. They offer me one. I say no. No input, without output.

“You’ll be fine,” says my husband, trying to reassure me unsuccessfully.

My throat is parched and my lips dry, but I decide to stay dehydrated for the next hour. As soon as we reach the destination, I begin searching for a toilet. I smell one before I spot it and decide to stay away. My daughter, who’s now beginning to show some empathy, joins in my search. So while the others admire the hills and the lake, and get ready for their boat rides, we scan the area for a toilet. Even after 15 minutes of frantic search, we don’t spot any. But we do notice a posh hotel nearby. My daughter looks at me with a glint in her eye. I get the hint. “Let’s go,” I tell her, “there’s no other way”.

So off we go into the hotel, walking past the freshly polished lobby towards the restaurant. Tables, chairs, potted plants, dessert displays and yes, there it is. A door with gents’ and ladies’ stick figures. Never in my life has a stick figure brought me so much joy.

While my daughter orders tea and cake, I scramble for the washroom. Ten minutes later, we step out of the hotel, my wallet lighter by a few hundred rupees, but my heart and bladder infinitely lighter. I was finally ready for the destination, now that I had survived the journey.
